planting.note: Divide clumps in early spring only when crowding reduces vigor; plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full to partial shade.

directions: This compact, densely clumping species carries thick, glaucous blue-green leaves in a tidy, uniform mound distinct from the larger sieboldiana-type hostas already common in cultivation. Its compact habit makes it well suited to shaded rock gardens or front-of-border placement rather than as a backdrop plant. It requires a genuine winter chill to break dormancy properly, turning yellow before going dormant, and resents frequent disturbance once established, so divide only when crowding clearly reduces vigor.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Divide congested clumps every 3-4 years in spring and plant into rich, humusy soil at a pond margin or other low spot that stays saturated through summer.

directions: Native from the eastern Himalaya through northwest Yunnan and northern Myanmar, this astilbe tolerates boggy, continuously wet soil better than most garden astilbe hybrids, making it a strong choice for pond margins or low spots that stay saturated through summer. Its thick branched rhizome produces taller, denser stem clusters than typical arendsii types, so give it more room than a standard border astilbe. Cut old growth back hard in early spring before new shoots emerge, and keep soil pH between 5.5 and 7 for best performance.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Divide congested clumps in late winter or early spring and plant in dappled shade with rich, humusy soil kept consistently moist.

directions: One of only two Astilbe species endemic to Korea, this plant produces looser, more relaxed flower plumes in white, lilac, or pale pink than the stiffly upright arendsii hybrids, giving a softer textural presence in a shaded border. It is notably drought intolerant and the foliage scorches quickly in hot sun or dry spells, so consistently moist or even boggy soil is essential. Because it is a regional Korean endemic rarely grown outside specialty perennial nurseries, source plants or seed from a reputable species-astilbe specialist to ensure correct identification.

planting.note: Divide only when clumps become difficult to manage, since mature specimens are large and heavy to move; give it the footprint of a small shrub in consistently moist, acidic soil.

directions: The largest-growing species in the genus, this astilbe dwarfs every other Astilbe in cultivation, with clumps spreading to five feet and flower spikes reportedly reaching six to seven feet — an exceptional architectural specimen for large shaded or woodland-edge plantings where most astilbes look too small-scale. New growth emerges with a bronze cast before maturing to dark green, giving useful spring color contrast ahead of its white summer plumes. Because of its exceptional size it works best as a specimen or back-of-border plant near streams or in woodland clearings rather than in a conventional mixed shade bed.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Divide clumps in spring and plant in a rock garden, trough, or edging position in moist but well-drained soil; avoid hot, exposed sites.

directions: A genuine miniature of the genus native to Yakushima Island, Japan, this astilbe forms a glossy, bronze-green mound of deeply divided, red-tinted foliage that stays attractive even out of bloom. Because of its small scale it is easily overwhelmed by larger neighbors and performs best in a rock garden, trough, or edging position rather than a mixed perennial border. It tolerates acid, neutral, or alkaline soils more readily than many other astilbes, broadening its usability across different garden soils, but like all astilbes it scorches quickly if allowed to dry out.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online
